title: What should you ask first in an M&A case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in an M&A case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Mergers and acquisitions cases have a reputation for being technical. In practice, they come down to a handful of plain questions.
body:
The first question to ask

Why does the client want to buy?

How to build your structure

  • Target on its own (its market, performance vs peers, standalone value)
  • Synergies (revenue, cost, minus integration costs)
  • Can we make it work? (funding, integration and culture, regulation)
  • Price (price vs value to us, other targets, build or partner instead)

The trap most people fall into

Ignoring integration risk and the do-nothing option.

For the full tree, with every branch, read the acquisition (M&A) framework.

Two prompts to try

Should a regional bakery chain buy a smaller rival for $60M?

Show a model structure
  • Target on its own: Its profits and growth; Value vs the $60M price
  • Synergies: Cost synergies: shared bakeries, buying, overheads; Revenue synergies: new regions, cross-selling
  • Risks: Integration, staff, customers lost; What we don't know: debts, contracts
  • Alternatives: Grow on our own; Buy a different target

Where to start: Standalone value vs price: synergies should be the bonus, not the reason.

The trap: Paying for synergies the buyer would have to deliver itself.

Should a coffee chain buy its main coffee roaster?

Show a model structure
  • Value of the roaster: Its profits, other customers; Price vs value
  • Benefits to us: Lower cost of beans, security of supply; Quality control
  • Risks: Losing the roaster's other customers; Running a factory, a new skill
  • Alternatives: Long-term contract; Minority stake

Where to start: Alternatives: a long contract may give most of the benefit without buying.

The trap: Assuming owning it is the only way to secure supply.
outro: Small things like this add up. Try it in your next practice case and notice how it changes the conversation. Practise this case type in the free casebook: every case has a worked answer.
